name: Tongkat ali
summary: Root extract of the Southeast Asian shrubby tree Eurycoma longifolia, long used as an aphrodisiac and taken mainly to raise testosterone; evidence comes from a few small trials.
what_it_is: Tongkat ali (Eurycoma longifolia) is a tall, slender, shrubby tree native to Southeast Asia, including Malaysia, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Myanmar. Its roots and bark have been used in traditional medicine for fever, malaria, coughs and many other conditions, and especially as an aphrodisiac. Its effects are attributed mainly to compounds called quassinoids, such as eurycomanone.

evidence.why: A 2022 meta-analysis of 5 small trials found higher total testosterone, mainly in men with low testosterone, but results varied widely and the trials were few and small.

status_us.label: Dietary supplement
status_us.note: Sold as a dietary supplement. A professional drug-information monograph notes that FDA does not consider Eurycoma longifolia generally recognized as safe (GRAS).

benefits.claim: Higher total testosterone than control in a 2022 meta-analysis of small trials; the rise was significant in men with low testosterone but not in men with normal levels, and results varied widely between trials
No clear improvement in erectile function versus placebo in 2 randomized trials (139 men) at high risk of bias; an older review counted benefit in 7 of 11 small studies of male sexual health
Better stress-hormone profile and some mood scores over 4 weeks in one study of 63 adults with moderate stress

risks.risk: Little is known about safety: trials were few and small, and side effects are poorly documented
Liver injury: it was among the single-ingredient supplements implicated in a US liver-injury network analysis
Hormonal effects: it can raise testosterone, and in rats it enlarged the prostate; it should not be used with prostate cancer
Contamination: one Malaysian product had higher-than-normal lead levels

interactions: Propranolol (a beta-blocker): tongkat ali may lower its blood levels

before: Total testosterone, if you are taking it for suspected low testosterone
labs.why: A testosterone test shows whether low testosterone is really the issue; yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or unusual tiredness should prompt liver tests.

studies.title: Eurycoma longifolia (Jack) Improves Serum Total Testosterone in Men: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Clinical Trials
studies.people: Men in 5 trials pooled as 7 comparisons (135 supplemented, 132 controls), with low or normal testosterone
studies.finding: Total testosterone rose overall and in men with low testosterone, but not significantly in men with normal levels; differences between trials were very large.

studies.title: Eurycoma Longifolia as a potential adoptogen of male sexual health: a systematic review on clinical studies
studies.people: 11 human studies of male sexual health published from 2000 to 2014
studies.finding: Seven studies reported a notable benefit and four did not; most were small randomized trials, cohort studies or pilot trials.

ask_your_clinician: Should my testosterone be tested before I try this, and is there an underlying cause to look for?
Is it safe with my prostate history or my medicines, including propranolol?
Which symptoms should make me stop and get liver tests?

sources.title: Eurycoma longifolia (Jack) Improves Serum Total Testosterone in Men: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Clinical Trials
Eurycoma Longifolia as a potential adoptogen of male sexual health: a systematic review on clinical studies
sources.publisher: Chinese Journal of Natural Medicines (WHO Global Index Medicus record)

notes_for_editor: Evidence rests on a few small trials, several sharing authors and most using one commercial extract (not named here); trial funding was not shown in the text read. The meta-analysis places one trial described as healthy volunteers in its low-testosterone subgroup, and very high heterogeneity makes the pooled estimate unstable. Safety, the propranolol interaction, lead contamination and the liver-injury signal come from a Drugs.com professional monograph (updated July 2026) rather than primary studies; no NIH or LiverTox page on tongkat ali was opened. The 2017 review was read only as an abstract, and its authors' conclusion of convincing evidence is stronger than its mixed results. The branded extract in the catalog aliases is not mentioned.
